extracted.intended_audience: Peer reviewers (manuscript reviewers) for PLOS and similar journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for peer reviewers on identifying, declaring, and managing competing interests when invited to review or while conducting a review. Covers types of competing interests, when and where to check, declaration procedures, and illustrative case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a competing interest?
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing interest is anything that interferes with, or could reasonably be perceived as interfering with, the full and objective presentation, peer review, editorial decision-making, or publication of research or non-research articles submitted to PLOS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competing interests can be financial or non-financial, professional, or personal, and can arise in relationship to an organization or another person. They matter because they can introduce perceived or actual bias in the submission or peer review process; the appearance of bias can compromise evaluation even if the study is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Could you profit or be negatively impacted financially by the submitted research?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the answer is yes, declare this as a competing interest to the journal before accepting the invitation to review. Check funding information in the submission to identify financial links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you have a personal relationship with the authors? Are you and the authors rivals or competitors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have personal relationships or direct rivalry/competition with the authors, declare these as competing interests to the journal before accepting. Personal relationships can reasonably be perceived as interfering with objective review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you recently worked at the same institution or organization as the authors? Have you or are you currently collaborating with the authors? Have you published with the authors during the last 5 years? Do you or have you held grants with the authors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These professional connections (including recent co-authorship within 5 years, past or current collaborations, shared institutional affiliation, or shared grants) should be declared if present; declare before accepting and re-check once you see submission files.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to check for competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: When you are invited to review a manuscript, check for any competing interests that may exist between you and the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask yourself the listed financial, personal, and professional questions at invitation time. If you accept to review, check again once you have access to all submission files (the author list, funding, acknowledgments, etc.), since new information may reveal additional conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where in the submission to look for competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Check key submission sections for information that may reveal competing interests: author list, funding information, acknowledgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author list: do you know any authors? Funding information: do you now, or have you recently, held grants with any of the authors? Acknowledgments: are you thanked in the acknowledgments? Use these sections to surface potential undeclared links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring competing interests to the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of the situations applies to you, or if you think you have a competing interest that’s not listed, get in touch with the journal right away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declare competing interests before accepting the invitation. Depending on the situation, editors may ask you to review anyway or may find a different reviewer. Early communication allows the editor to make an informed decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring competing interests in reviewer comments if retained
rubrics_metrics.description: If the journal editors decide to keep you as a reviewer on the manuscript, they will probably ask you to declare the competing interest in your reviewer comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the declaration in your comments makes your position transparent so the editor can account for relationships and perceived bias when evaluating your feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing interests are not necessarily disqualifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Competing interests are not necessarily bad. It’s okay to have them. The important thing is that they are declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaration ensures the editor understands the relationships in play and can account for them when weighing reviewer feedback; disclosure preserves integrity even if the reviewer believes they can be objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative case studies of problematic undisclosed competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-life examples showing how undisclosed interests can create problems: (1) Reviewer recommends rejection, then submits a manuscript to the same journal on the same topic. (2) Reviewer suggests rejecting a manuscript and turns out to be affiliated with a competing institution, which was not disclosed. (3) Reviewer recommends rejection and turns out to have a patent on a method challenged by the submitted research, which was not disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These case studies (from COPE and WAME) illustrate why nondisclosure can bias decisions or create the appearance of bias; if you encounter similar situations, contact the journal for advice and disclose relevant information.
